Percussion is the biggest family in the band by number of instruments, and the one where a single player is most likely to switch
between several in one piece. This lesson is the common ground: how to pick up a stick, how a stroke is made, how to play the
concert bass drum, and how any drum is looked after and tuned. The [snare drum](snare-drum.qmd) has its own page, with the parts,
the rudiments and a player that sounds them.

## What the section covers {#section}

The teacher book's percussion chapter lists these topics, in this order: the world of percussion, percussion notation, selecting
players, technique fundamentals, snare drum / bass drum / toms / tenor drum, mallet percussion, tonal and coloristic effect
instruments, timpani, cymbals / gong / tam-tam, triangle, tambourine, shakers and rattles, blocks / cowbell / claves / castanets,
drum set, the school percussion section, the Percussive Arts Society's rudiments, and a keyboard layout chart for mallet
instruments. Only some of that is on this site so far:

## Sticks, mallets and beaters {#implements}

Most percussion instruments are played with something held in the hand: a stick, a mallet or a beater. The size, weight and
material of that tool change the sound a great deal, and some techniques cannot be done with the wrong one. A snare drum roll will
not work with yarn mallets, and snare sticks are no use when a part asks for brushes. Learn early to choose **the right tool for the
job**.

## Grip {#grip}

*Grip* is how you hold the stick or mallet. Two are in common use.

- **Matched grip:** both hands hold the stick the same way.
- **Traditional grip:** the hands hold it differently. It began as a way to hold the left stick when a drum hung from a strap at
  the player's side, so the drum sat at a slant. Concert stands were made to tilt a drum to the same angle, and the habit came
  with them.

The book's advice is to start beginners, even on snare drum, with **matched grip**, for these reasons:

1. A percussionist has to be able to play nearly everything, and matched grip works on almost all of it.
2. The same hold in both hands means fewer things to learn. Traditional grip tends to need a lot of extra practice for the left hand.
3. It is more natural for most beginners (though a teacher still has to check it is correct, not just natural).
4. The two hands look alike, so the sound is easier to even out.
5. Marching bands today mostly use a carrier that holds the drum level, so the old reason for the slant has gone.
6. The arm, hand and wrist motions are the same as those used when playing with the hands, which is a skill needed for a lot of
   instruments.

When you start on **mallet percussion**, matched grip is the only choice. Traditional grip is still worth knowing: a student may
have learned it from another teacher, or a local marching band may use it, and then the book suggests teaching it alongside
matched grip so progress on the other instruments is not held up.

Step by step, [matched grip](snare-drum.qmd#grip) and traditional grip are on the snare drum page.

## The four basic strokes {#strokes}

A stroke has three parts: the stick moves **toward** the surface, **strikes** it, and moves **away**, using the natural bounce. It
comes mostly from the fingers, hand and wrist; some arm movement is fine. The four basic strokes differ in where the stick starts
and where it ends up.

| Stroke | Starts | Ends | Sounds and used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Full** (F) | 45–90° above the surface | back where it started | Often accented; any dynamic |
| **Down** (D) | 45–90° above | low, near the surface: the hand stops the rebound | Often accented; going from loud to soft |
| **Up** (u) | near the surface | 45–90° above | Not accented; going from soft to loud |
| **Tap** (t) | near the surface | near the surface | Soft, unaccented |

Which one you use depends on how loud the note must be and where the stick has to be for the next note. Practise combinations of
F, D, u and t one hand at a time until each hand makes each stroke equally well. The same ideas return when you read about
[flams](snare-drum.qmd#flams): the quiet grace note is a tap, and in alternating flams the grace is an up stroke and the main note
a down stroke.

## The bass drum {#bass-drum}

The concert bass drum sits on a stand with wheels, tilted toward the player. Click a part, or press **Quiz me**.

::: {#pc-bass data-kind="bass"}
:::

### Mallet and set-up

- Use a **felt-covered bass drum mallet** with a heavy, weighted feel. Hold it between the first joint of the index finger and the
  pad of the thumb, as you would a snare stick, and let the other fingers steer.
- **Lock the wheels** and tilt the drum. The angle depends on the music and what is comfortable.
- Stand behind the drum and a little to the right of it, with your weight even on both feet. Stand on a small riser, step or stool
  if you need one to line up with the drum.

### Playing it

1. Strike the batter head **off-centre** for a deep, dark, open sound. Use a direct forearm and wrist movement, then **lift the
   mallet straight off** so the sound is drawn out of the drum. Avoid glancing, circular or figure-eight movements.
2. Dead centre gives a dead tone, and close to the rim a thin one. They are useful in some music but are not the usual way to play.
3. A concert bass drum rings after you hit it. Let it, or for a drier, crisper sound **dampen** the head with your fingers.

### Dampening

- The free hand's fingers are the first choice. A small hand towel, or even a soft oven mitt on that hand, also works.
- If the drum is tilted close to upright, the **knee** can press on the head: rest the right foot on the stand or a stool and press the
  knee on the batter head. This suits a stream of short notes, such as a march or show tune where the drum doubles a quarter-note
  bass line. The left hand can also muffle the resonant head.
- Dampening **after** the stroke (let it sound for a moment, then stop it) is often better than damping before, even on short
  notes where you want a full sound at the moment of impact. Listen to the other bass instruments to decide how much to damp.

### Rolls

Use a **matched pair** of bass drum mallets made for rolling, the same size, style and weight. Hit the head between the centre and the
rim with alternating slow to moderately slow single strokes, both mallets the same distance from the rim. Tilting the drum makes
the roll easier. Rolls are usually played with matched grip (traditional also works, for a softer effect). In **concert**
playing only the batter head is used; a marching bass drum is different, with a hand on each head.

### Bass drum checklist

- Weight even on both feet?
- Body in the right position for the drum?
- Mallet held correctly?
- Striking the right place on the head?
- Right stroke technique?
- Good tone?

## Changing a drum head {#heads}

Most drum maintenance is changing or tuning heads. Replace a head that is old, worn, dented or punctured even if it has not broken
(batter heads need changing more often than the bottom heads), and keep spares, because heads break at any time. Before the late 1950s
heads were made of animal skin; plastic heads are the better choice for most playing now, but use a head made for the drum's job
(a marching head can be too thick for concert work).

The book's procedure for a snare, bass or tom head:

1. With a **drum key**, take out each tension rod, then lift off the rim(s) and the head(s). Take the snares off too if the bottom head is
   coming off.
2. Clear out dirt from inside the drum; tighten or replace any loose screws, nuts or bolts on the shell.
3. Wipe the edge of the shell.
4. Clean the lugs and tension rods and put on a little light household lubricant.
5. Fit the new head, put the rim back and run the rods in. Tighten first with the fingers, then with the key, in a **criss-cross**
   order: tighten opposite rods one after another, **no more than a half turn on each** before moving on, and repeat until all the
   slack is out.
6. If you need to, seat the head by pressing the centre lightly with your fingers or the heel of your hand.
7. Tune it (below), and make small adjustments daily for a week or two, which helps the heads hold their tuning and last longer.
8. Reattach the snares on a snare drum if you took them off.

### The tightening order {#tuning-order}

The book's figure numbers ten lugs round a head from 1 to 10. The lugs that follow each other (1 and 2, 3 and 4, …) are on opposite
sides of the head. Reading the numbers as the order to tighten them is this site's reading of the figure; the text says only "criss-cross".
Step through it.

::: {#pc-tuning}
:::

## Tuning and muffling {#tuning}

Tune the heads whenever you change them, and now and then after that to keep the drum sounding its best.

1. Set the drum on a towel or soft surface to deaden the bottom head. **Tap the batter head** two or three inches from each tension
   rod (with the snares off, on a snare drum) and adjust in small steps, with the criss-cross order, until every point gives exactly the
   same pitch and a clear, resonant sound. On a snare the head should also bounce back well.
2. Turn the drum over and do the same for the bottom head. On a snare drum, put a soft cloth or foam between the snares and the head
   in the middle to mute the snares, and take care not to over-tighten that thin head.
3. On a snare, after the heads are done, adjust the snares until it is crisp and responsive at every dynamic.

**How high?** Depends on the drum's natural range. Too tight and the drum sounds choked and loses its depth; too loose and it
sounds flabby, with little tone or stick response.

**Two heads, two pitches.** Either both heads are tuned to the same pitch, or one is higher than the other. Try both. On a snare drum,
the snare (bottom) head is generally higher than the batter head, usually by about a perfect fourth or fifth. On a bass drum, the
book suggests the batter head low and the resonant head higher, or both the same, so the drum is deep and resonant with no clear
pitch. A bass drum tuned to a definite note will sooner or later clash with the rest of the band.

**Muffling.** The less muffling, the bigger, richer and fuller the sound, so use as little as you can, especially on a concert bass
drum. Options include plastic film rings (snare, toms and tenor drums), gaffer's tape, paper towels, foam rubber, felt strips and
special mufflers. Near the outer edge of the head usually works best, and it is better to make it temporary (a handkerchief, or
removable gel patches), so you can adjust it to the music. Some drums have a built-in muffler worked by a knob.

The book ends this section with a reminder that drum tuning and muffling are a matter of personal taste, and that what it gives is
a starting point.
